title: How Traffic Light Sensors Work in 60 Seconds 🚦🚗 #shorts
description:
Many traffic lights know a car is waiting thanks to an inductive loop: a coil of wire cut into the road. A detector runs alternating current through it, and a car's metal underside changes the loop's inductance and frequency, so the controller knows to give you a green light. Follow Inside 60 for a new "how it works" explained in 60 seconds.

#trafficlight #engineering #howitworks

steps.label: Hook
steps.text: That traffic light may know you're waiting because of a *wire loop* buried in the road.

steps.label: Loop
steps.text: Thin cuts in the asphalt hold a few turns of wire, forming a big *coil*.

steps.label: Field
steps.text: A detector sends *alternating current* through it, making a *magnetic field* above the road.

steps.label: Car
steps.text: A car's *metal underside* disturbs that field, so the loop's *frequency* shifts.

steps.label: Bikes
steps.text: Bicycles have less metal, so many loops have a marked *sweet spot* — stop right on top of the *wire*.

steps.label: Signal
steps.text: The detector spots the shift and tells the *controller* a car is waiting. Time for *green*.

steps.label: Recap
steps.text: Loop, field, *green light*. Follow Inside 60 for more.
